ca_alien_head_area.blurb: Alien Head Area is a small group of formations on the hillside above Rattlesnake Wash, in the Indian Cove and Rattlesnake Canyon corner of Joshua Tree National Park. It has nine routes, eight bolted and one trad, graded from 5.8 up to 5.10, which suits climbers working through the lower end of the tens. Rock quality swings widely from one line to the next, and the darker stone tends to be the sounder choice. The routes sit in a notch between two hills, reached by a steep uphill walk with loose gravel underfoot.

ca_memorial_wall_2.blurb: Memorial Wall is a limestone wall in Cave Valley, the old quarry climbing zone inside Auburn State Recreation Area. It has nine climbs: eight sport routes and a single V3 boulder problem. The sport lines run from 5.7 to 5.11, with most clustered around 5.9 and 5.10. The rock is near-vertical to vertical, and the routes are short compared with the other walls in the valley. The wall turns shady in the afternoon, which makes it a useful retreat when the neighboring walls are baking. It is the darker rock immediately to the right as you enter the valley.

ca_crag_full_of_dynamite.blurb: Crag Full of Dynamite is a small sandstone crag beside East Camino Cielo, the ridge road above Santa Barbara, with a view north over Los Padres National Forest. It has nine routes: six bolted lines and three top-rope climbs, graded 5.7 to 5.9, with 5.8 the most common. The stone is soft, so treat holds gently. The wall faces north, which keeps it cold through winter, so spring and fall are the best times to visit. The walk from the road is minimal and the crag gives about half a day of climbing.

ca_cap_rock_southeast_face.blurb: This is the slabby face on Cap Rock, a short walk from the Cap Rock lot off Keys View Road in Joshua Tree National Park. It has nine routes: six trad and three top-rope, running from 5.6 to 5.10, with four of them at 5.10. The lower-grade lines make it a reasonable place to bring newer climbers who want top-rope laps, while the harder trad lines add variety. The leftmost routes catch sun all day and are sheltered from wind, which makes the face a good pick on a cold winter day.

ca_crystal_skull.blurb: Crystal Skull is an isolated dome near the south end of Bighorn Pass Road, close to Queen Mountain in Joshua Tree National Park, at roughly 4,400 feet. The rock carries very large crystals, and the north face is unusually smooth. Nine problems are spread around the dome, running from the easiest grades up to V3, with a spread of VB through V2 that suits newer boulderers. A smaller boulder nearby has a cave-like hollow. Plan on a dirt-road drive and pullouts beside the formation rather than a lot or trailhead.

ca_campfire_crag_boulder.blurb: Campfire Crag Boulder is a single boulder below Campfire Crag, set among the campsites of Indian Cove in Joshua Tree National Park. It has nine problems on monzogranite, ranging from VB to V4, with the largest group at VB. That makes it friendly for beginners and for warming up, with a few harder problems on the far side of the boulder for anyone who wants a bigger challenge. It is a short session rather than a full day, and it pairs well with the other boulders scattered around the campground.

ca_the_cathouse_middle.blurb: The middle section of the Cathouse, a small formation beside Playhouse Rock in the Lost Horse area of Joshua Tree National Park. It has nine routes, eight trad and one top-rope, graded from 5.5 up to 5.9. The wall is a sheltered mix of cracks and faces, with tan rock broken by brown patina patches. Routes are short, the formation sees little traffic, and some stretches are loose, so check holds as you go. The grades make it a fair spot for climbers building trad experience on easier ground.
ca_the_cathouse_middle.parking_note: Leave the car at the Playhouse Rock turnout in the Lost Horse area; the Cathouse formation is the one beside Playhouse Rock.
ca_the_cathouse_middle.approach: A trail from the turnout leads to the base of the formation, then you continue along the wall to the middle section.

ca_big_bender_crag.blurb: Big Bender Crag is a south-facing cliff in Lee Vining Canyon, off the Tioga Road in the Eastern Sierra, at about 7,960 feet. It has nine routes, eight bolted and one trad, from 5.8 to 5.11, with seven of them at 5.10. Most of the development is recent, and the anchors are set up for friendly lowering and rappelling. Facing south and sitting this high, the crag works best in the shoulder seasons and on mild winter days, when the canyon below stays comfortable and the wall gets good sun.
